qs.q: A 60-year-old man has had abdominal pain and early satiety for 8 months. He has a history of Helicobacter pylori gastritis. Endoscopy shows a gastric mucosal mass. Biopsy shows a low-grade B-cell lymphoma composed of small lymphocytes infiltrating the mucosa. Most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: H. pylori gastritis + low-grade B-cell mucosal lymphoma = gastric MALT lymphoma (marginal zone lymphoma). H. pylori antigen chronically stimulates mucosal B cells leading to clonal proliferation. Early cases may regress with H. pylori eradication.

qs.q: Which enzyme produced by Helicobacter pylori helps it survive in the acidic stomach?
qs.e: H. pylori produces urease, which hydrolyzes urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide, helping buffer the acidic environment around the organism.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Helicobacter pylori is a spiral, urease‑producing bacterium that colonises the gastric mucosa, causing chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease and increasing gastric cancer risk. Its survival depends on urease‑mediated neutralisation of acid and adhesins that bind to epithelial cells.

sections.p: H. pylori is a microaerophilic, spiral bacterium that colonises the human stomach. It is the most common cause of chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease worldwide.

The bacterium uses urease to hydrolyse urea, producing ammonia that neutralises gastric acid, allowing it to survive in the acidic environment. Adhesins such as BabA and SabA bind to gastric epithelial cells, promoting colonisation.

t.b: Detects active infection by measuring ammonia production; a positive result indicates urease‑producing organisms in the biopsy.

sections.p: Transmission is primarily fecal‑oral, often via contaminated food or water. The bacterium persists in the gastric mucosa, forming microcolonies that evade immune clearance.

t.b: Detects H. pylori antigens in stool; positive indicates active infection, useful when endoscopy is unavailable.

sections.p: H. pylori infection leads to chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, gastric carcinoma and MALT lymphoma. Symptoms range from epigastric pain to dyspepsia and, in severe cases, bleeding.

t.b: Confirms gastritis and visualises organisms; guides diagnosis when non‑invasive tests are inconclusive.

sections.p: Diagnosis combines non‑invasive tests (urea breath, stool antigen) and invasive tests (biopsy for histology, rapid urease, culture).

t.b: Answers whether urease‑producing organisms are present in biopsy; a positive result confirms infection.
Answers presence of inflammation and organisms; helps stage gastritis severity.

sections.p: First‑line therapy is a triple or quadruple regimen that includes a proton pump inhibitor and two antibiotics. The choice of antibiotics depends on local resistance patterns.

t.b: Determines resistance to clarithromycin or metronidazole; guides choice of regimen when available.

sections.p: Remember that H. pylori is urease positive, adheres via BabA/SabA, and is the main cause of peptic ulcer relapse. In low‑resource settings, stool antigen or rapid urease are practical diagnostics.
